chapter_en: The Laws of the Murderer and of Suicide

sections.title_en: 1. The Punishment of a Deliberate Murderer
sections.body_en:
According to Torah law, if the guilt of the murderer was proven by valid witnesses, the beit din is obligated to sentence him to death. It is important to note that only rarely did they carry out a death sentence on a person who sinned; therefore our Sages said that any Sanhedrin that executed one person in seven years was called a "destructive Sanhedrin", because it did not act with deliberation in judgement. And in the view of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, even if it executed one in seventy years it was already called a "destructive Sanhedrin" (Makkot 1:10). In any case, for those rare cases in which they did pass a death sentence, precise halakhot were stated as to how each criminal is executed.

There are four forms of execution: stoning, burning, the sword and strangulation.[1] The deliberate murderer is sentenced to death by the sword, which was carried out by cutting off the murderer's head with a sword (Sanhedrin 7:3).

There is a special law regarding putting the murderer to death: all the other death sentences were carried out by the witnesses or the officers of the beit din, whereas carrying out the sentence on the murderer was done by the blood-avenger, as it is said (Bamidbar 35:21): "The blood-avenger shall put the murderer to death." And anyone fit to inherit the murdered person is considered the blood-avenger. But this is not indispensable: if the murdered person has no relatives, or they do not wish to put the murderer to death with their own hands, the beit din would appoint an agent on its behalf to carry out the sentence.

So important is it to fence off the terrible breach of the sin of murder that the Torah specially warned the beit din that under no circumstances should it agree to accept ransom from a murderer sentenced to death. And even if the murderer asks to redeem his life for vast wealth, and promises to donate it for the benefit of the poor and needy, and even if the family of the murdered person beg on his behalf not to put him to death – the beit din is commanded to put him to death. All this because there is no measure to the value of human life, and all the money in the world is not worth one soul. Therefore the Torah was stricter about the sin of bloodshed than about any other sin (Rambam, Laws of the Murderer 1:4).

And likewise we learned about the great severity of murder and the loss of human life from the law of the egla arufa, the heifer whose neck is broken, by which the elders of the town must atone for themselves for a murder having happened in their place without their having punished the murderer (see Peninei Halakha, "The Nation and the Land" 7:2).

notes_en.en: This is also the order of their severity: for the most severe sins against Heaven one is punished by stoning – for example, an idol worshipper is punished by stoning; for less severe ones by burning, for less than that by the sword, and the death considered lightest is death by strangulation. And although the murderer is punished only by the third death in severity, this is because from the aspect of rebellion against Hashem there are more severe transgressions, such as idolatry. But from the aspect of the destruction of the world, the murderer's sin is the most severe of all, as the Rambam wrote in Hilkhot Rotze'aḥ chapter 4, halakha 9, and as will be explained in the next halakha.

sections.title_en: 2. Stringency in Punishing a Deliberate Murderer
sections.body_en:
We have learned that it is a mitzva to be very deliberate in capital cases, and in practice death sentences were hardly ever carried out.

The halakhic reason for this is that for all the sins whose punishment is death, they would not execute the accused unless the witnesses had warned him before the act, for example by saying to him: "Know that if you commit this sin you will be punished by such-and-such a death in the beit din." And only if he said to them, "Even so I will sin," and sinned, could he be punished by death in the beit din. In addition, the rules of examining and cross-examining the witnesses were hard and stringent, and if a small contradiction was found between the testimony of the two witnesses, even in a marginal detail – even though it was entirely clear to the beit din that the transgression had been committed – nevertheless they would not pass a death sentence as long as the testimony of the witnesses was not entirely identical in all its details. Therefore, even people who sinned with idolatry and forbidden relations were almost always exempt from death. And as we learned in the previous halakha, a Sanhedrin that executed one person in seven years is called "destructive" (Makkot 1:10).

But regarding a deliberate murderer there is a special law. Whenever it is clear to the beit din that this person indeed deliberately murdered his fellow, even though formally, according to the rules of the laws of execution by beit din, it is not possible to punish him with the regular death, which is killing by the sword, nevertheless, since it is clear to them beyond a shadow of doubt that this criminal murdered, they would cause him to die in an indirect way. They would put him in prison and feed him sparingly with scant bread and scant water until his stomach shrank. After that they would give him an unlimited amount of barley foods to eat, and since his intestines had shrunk, they were not able to digest large quantities of food, and so by his eating he would bring about his own death.

And so the Rambam wrote (Laws of the Murderer 4:9): "This is not done to others who are liable to death by beit din; rather, if he is liable to death, they put him to death, and if he is not liable to death, they release him. For although there are sins (from the aspect of rebellion against Hashem) more severe than bloodshed, there is not in them the destruction of the settlement of the world as there is in bloodshed. Even idolatry, and needless to say forbidden relations or desecration of Shabbat, are not like bloodshed, for these sins are transgressions between a person and the Holy One, blessed be He, but bloodshed is among the transgressions between a person and his fellow; and whoever has this sin on his hands is a complete wicked man, and all the mitzvot he did all his days do not weigh against this sin, and will not save him from judgement…"

sections.title_en: 3. More on the Severity of the Sin of Murder and Its Punishment
sections.body_en:
Not only the one who killed with his own hands must be punished; rather, the one who sent agents to kill a person, or who set a predatory beast upon his fellow, the beit din is also obligated to punish, because he is a partner in the murder. And as the Rambam wrote (Laws of the Murderer 2:5), one must "strike them a severe blow close to death, imprison them in siege and distress for many years, and afflict them with all kinds of affliction, in order to frighten and deter the other wicked."

And not only this, but in rare cases, if the beit din saw that the generation was rife with murder, and there was a need to set up a fence against murders, it was possible to punish, not according to the rules of law, even one about whom there was no valid testimony, or who only caused the murder. This mode of punishment is called "the law of the king". That is, generally they would act according to the rules of the law of the Sanhedrin written in the Torah, which are eternal rules. But sometimes there was a need to depart from the routine rules, and for this the king had the authority to punish exceptionally, even with the death penalty. When there is no king, the ordained beit din can act according to the law of the king and punish offenders exceptionally, in order to fight crime (SA ḤM 2:1).

The reason for the stringency in the murderer's punishment is that the value of human life is above all measure and value, and therefore one must not keep silent about so terrible an act as the murder of a person. Therefore, as long as murderers are left unpunished, as it were the whole land is defiled, and the blood cries out to heaven without atonement. And so it is said (Bamidbar 35:33-34): "So you shall not pollute the land in which you are, for blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it except by the blood of him who shed it. And you shall not defile the land in which you dwell, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the Lord dwell in the midst of the Children of Israel."

And likewise the Sages said (Sanhedrin 37a) that all humanity began from one man, to teach us the value of each individual: "For whoever destroys one soul of Israel, Scripture considers it as though he destroyed an entire world, and whoever sustains one soul of Israel, Scripture considers it as though he sustained an entire world." And likewise we find that after Kayin killed Hevel, it was said to him (Bereshit 4:10): "The bloods of your brother cry out," in the plural, to teach us that not only his blood cries out from the ground, but also the blood of all the generations that could have been born from him had he not been murdered – cry out from the ground.

As is known, there are three transgressions whose severity is greater than the severity of all other transgressions, and they are: idolatry, forbidden relations and bloodshed. And so severe are they that a person is obligated to give up his life rather than transgress one of them. For example, if wicked murderers come and threaten a person and put two options before him – either transgress one of the three transgressions, or we will kill you – he is obligated to sanctify Hashem's Name and be killed rather than transgress.

Regarding the prohibition of murder, it is clear to anyone who has a trace of morality that a person is forbidden to kill his fellow in order to save himself; for why should he consider his own life preferable to his fellow's life?! Or, in the language of the Talmud, why should his own blood be considered redder than his fellow's blood (Sanhedrin 74a)? Therefore it is clear that a person is forbidden to kill his fellow in order to save himself.

Even if gentiles come and threaten a group of people, "If you do not give us one person so that we may kill him, we will kill all of you," even in such a case they are forbidden to hand over one of their fellows to be killed in order to save themselves. And one may not argue: but if we hand over our fellow to be killed, thereby the lives of ten Jews will be saved, and if we do not hand him over to be killed, eleven Jews will be killed in the end. The reason for this is that the life of every person has an absolute and infinite value. Therefore it is not possible to say that one infinity is greater than another infinity. And according to the same halakhic logic, it is clear that one may not kill a person in order to take organs from him to save several people (Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:5).

The truth is that also from the aspect of the general consideration, it is clear that it is better that the whole group be killed rather than hand over one of them to be killed. For when the value of life begins to be legal tender, and the absolute fence before the prohibition "You shall not murder" is breached, murders will multiply, and in the end many more people will be killed. But according to halakha it is clear that even if we knew with certainty that handing over a person to be killed in order to save the rest of the group would not harm the general moral system, even then it would be forbidden to hand him over to be killed, because of the absolute value of human life, for we have no permission in any way to cause the death of an innocent person.

However, if one person volunteers of his own will to give himself up to death in order to save the rest of the group, according to several poskim he fulfils a mitzva by this, and it is a trait of piety (Ta'anit 18b, as in the incident of the martyrs of Lod).

However, if a person's strength did not hold and he failed, and preferred to kill his fellow in order to save himself – although he murdered, he is not punished with death as though he were an ordinary murderer, because he carried out the murder under duress. And apparently his sentence would be determined by the judgement of the judges (Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 5:4).

Not only one who murdered deliberately is punished, but even a person who killed unintentionally is punished. According to the Torah, his punishment is that he must leave his place of residence and go into exile to one of the cities of refuge designated for this. And he had to stay there until the death of the High Priest who served at that time. If the unintentional killer left the city of refuge before the death of the High Priest, the blood-avenger, that is, one of the relatives of the person killed, was permitted to kill him (Bamidbar 35:9-32).

The reason for this is that in fact even an act done unintentionally is done out of some kind of inner consent. For example, if it happened that a person forgot the day of Shabbat and did work on it, it is a sign that Shabbat is not so precious to him, and therefore he forgot it. Likewise, a person who was not careful and ate forbidden food by mistake – it is a sign that keeping kashrut is not important enough to him. And likewise a person who happened to kill his fellow unintentionally – it is a sign that human life is not precious to him, and therefore he was not careful not to harm his fellow. Therefore even a person who sinned unintentionally must atone for his sin.

And since murder is such a severe and terrible thing, a person must be seven times as careful not to harm his fellow, and if he was not careful, his punishment is more severe. And unlike the other severe sins, where for one who transgresses them unintentionally it is enough to bring a sin-offering to atone for his sin, the unintentional killer must change his whole life: he must go into exile to the city of refuge, and correct his character there, so that he and others will always be careful not to harm, God forbid, the life of their fellow. And if he does not do so, the blood-avenger will be permitted to kill him.

Today none of the laws of the unintentional killer apply. For the basic condition for all this is that the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one elders sit in its place in Jerusalem and be able to judge capital cases. And another condition must also be fulfilled: that all six cities of refuge – three of them on the western side of the Jordan and three on the eastern side – be set apart and dedicated to this purpose (Ḥinukh 410; Rambam, Laws of the Murderer 8:2).

Every person who caused the death of his fellow, as soon as it became clear to him that his fellow had been killed, would begin to flee quickly to one of the cities of refuge, so that the blood-avengers – the relatives of the person killed – would not be able to catch him and kill him. From the moment he reached the cities of refuge he was saved from the blood-avengers; but the beit din would send for him and bring him before the Sanhedrin. And they would escort him on his way to the beit din, in order to prevent the blood-avengers from harming him. If it became clear in the beit din that the killing had been carried out deliberately, they would execute the murderer; and if it became clear that he killed unintentionally, they would return him to the city of refuge.

Although only six cities were called cities of refuge, in fact all the cities of the Levites were cities of refuge. But the difference was that if the killer chose to live in one of the six cities of refuge, he did not have to pay rent for his dwelling; but if he chose to live in one of the remaining forty-two cities of the Levites, he had to pay rent for his dwelling (Rambam, Laws of the Murderer 8:9-10).

The period of his exile was intended to atone for his sin and correct his character. Therefore the killers had to avoid honour. If people wanted to honour one of the killers with something, the killer had to say to them: "I am a killer." And if they nevertheless wanted to honour him, he was permitted to accept the honour (Rambam, Laws of the Murderer 7:7). The reason the exile was conducted specifically in the cities of the Levites was so that the period of exile would have educational value. As is known, the Levites were appointed over matters of the spirit and education in the people of Israel, and therefore their cities were scattered among all the inheritances of the tribes of Israel, so that they could influence the whole public. And there in the city of refuge, that unintentional killer would regret his carelessness and correct his ways.

It is also important to know that one of the purposes of the city of refuge was to remove the unintentional killer from his area of residence, in order to calm the conflict that might erupt between the family of the killer and that of the person killed – a conflict which among many peoples would generally create a terrible snowball of blood revenge from both families. By contrast, staying among the Levites, the people of the spirit, gave security that the blood-avengers would not reach there, since they would not dare to violate the sacred rules of the cities of refuge. And so the quarrel was stopped at its root.

Many explain that the reason the killer had to live there until the day of the High Priest's death is that, according to the High Priest's lofty spiritual level, he ought to have influenced blessing and morality on all Israel, so that something as terrible as an unintentional killing would not happen in the people of Israel. And if nevertheless it happened, it implies that the service of the Temple was not performed by him with the proper completeness.

Since the day of release of the unintentional killers depended on the death of the High Priest, there was a concern that the killers would pray for the High Priest to die, so that they could be released from exile and return to their place of residence. Therefore, every Erev Yom Kippur, the mothers of the High Priests were accustomed to honour the killers with kinds of food, so that they would not pray for the death of their son, the High Priest.

There are three kinds of unintentional acts: the first is an error done out of negligence; the second, a complete error; and the third, an error close to compulsion.

The error close to negligence is that of one who was not careful in his actions and did something dangerous, and in the end a person was killed by his actions. For example: one who threw a stone into the public domain and it struck a person and killed him, or one who knocks down a wall in the middle of the day towards the street. Although he did not intend to kill, since from the outset he did a grave act with shameful carelessness, his act is therefore considered an error close to negligence, and his law is more severe, in that the city of refuge does not help to atone for him. Therefore, if the blood-avenger found him and killed him, he was exempt from any punishment (Rambam, Laws of the Murderer 6:4-6).

The ordinary unintentional killer is one who was reasonably careful, and nevertheless it happened that he killed a person. For example: while he swung the axe to strike the tree, from the momentum of the blow the iron came loose from the handle, struck his fellow's head and killed him; and likewise if he was going down a ladder and suddenly a rung broke and he fell on another person and killed him. In all these he is considered an unintentional killer. On the one hand it is clear that there is no negligence in him, and on the other hand it is reasonable that had he been more careful, he would not have killed his fellow. Therefore his punishment is that he go into exile to the city of refuge until the death of the High Priest.

The error close to compulsion is that of one who, even had he been very careful, could not have prevented the killing. For example: a person who knocked down a wall inside his own courtyard, and a person entered there without his permission, and a stone struck him and killed him. Or a person who meant to swing an axe, and as he raised the axe backwards, the iron suddenly came loose and flew behind him and struck a person there and killed him. This is a rare case, because the raising of the axe is done without much force, and it is very rare that the iron comes loose from the handle then and flies off. In such cases the error is close to compulsion, because the danger in them could not be foreseen, and it is therefore hard to take precautions to prevent it. Therefore one who kills by an error close to compulsion is exempt from exile to the city of refuge, and of course the blood-avenger is forbidden to kill him (based on the Rambam there 6:11-14).

In any case, it is clear that even a person who killed under compulsion ought to be stirred to teshuva. For the very fact that from Heaven such a terrible thing came about through him is a sign that there is a flaw in him, and he must correct his ways.

sections.title_en: 8. Remedy for an Unintentional Killer After the Cities of Refuge Ceased
sections.body_en:
After the destruction of the Land and the Temple, the laws of the unintentional killer ceased. On the one hand, the blood-avenger has no permission to kill the killer; and on the other hand, there is no set atonement for the terrible sin of the unintentional killer.

Nevertheless, when it happened to a Jew that a person was killed through him, and he wanted to atone for his sin, he would come to one of the great sages of Israel so that he would arrange for him an order of teshuva to atone for his sin. And in each and every case, according to the severity of the act and the person's strength, the great sages of Israel would advise the sinners how to atone for their sin.

Of all the many responsa on the subject, I will mention one responsum of the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger, who was one of the great poskim of the Aḥaronim. This is because his responsum deals with a case similar to the road accidents of our day, for, regrettably, most unintentional killings in our day occur through accidents.

And this is what happened: a certain man ran over his son and his servant with his wagon, which was harnessed to horses. Of course the thing was done unintentionally; but nevertheless, since such a terrible thing was done through him – and as is known, our Sages said (Shabbat 32a) that merit is brought about through the meritorious and guilt through the guilty – he therefore asked Rabbi Akiva Eiger how he should atone for his transgression and return in teshuva.

Since that man was wealthy, the rabbi answered that to atone for the killing of his son, he should allocate to a tzedaka fund the whole sum he had been prepared to give for his son's wedding, and with the profits from this fund he should support a son of poor people, and pay for his tuition, and the cost of his food and clothing, and so maintain him until he was fifteen. After that he should take another poor child under his patronage, and so continue all his life. And if those poor children married, he should ask them to name their first son after his son who was killed. In order to atone for the killing of the servant, he should allocate another large sum to a tzedaka fund, and from the profits of the fund pay tuition for children of the poor. And in the first year, he should pay ten people to study a lesson every day for the elevation of his soul.

In addition, he set for him an order of fasts: that in the first year he should fast much, and afterwards reduce his fasts. He also instructed that he should not go to wedding celebrations for all the days of his life, except the weddings of his children and grandchildren. And every night before sleep he should confess his sin. And on the anniversary of the death of the son and the servant, he should gather a minyan of ten, who would pray at their grave and ask forgiveness on his behalf.

And Rabbi Akiva Eiger concludes that in the merit of this teshuva of his, that sin would be forgiven him, and even the souls of those killed would be appeased and would intercede favourably for him, and he would merit length of days and to raise his children in joy to Torah and service (Responsa of Rabbi Akiva Eiger, Mahadura Tinyana, siman 3).

Today, one who is punished with imprisonment for his negligence already has suffering in place of fasts; but there is still no substitute here for the good deeds and tzedaka and Torah study that it is fitting for him to do for the elevation of the soul of the one killed through him and for the sake of his family, in order to repair his sin. And there are many who, although they killed unintentionally, came out completely acquitted in court; and in order to atone for their sin, they must take upon themselves suffering, similar to the suffering of one exiled to a city of refuge. Therefore, today too, it is fitting for one who killed a person to consult a rabbi so that he will arrange for him an order of teshuva and repair for his sin.

sections.title_en: 9. The Severity of the Prohibition, and When It Is Permitted
sections.body_en:
The prohibition of suicide is one of the most severe sins, and one who takes his own life is considered an actual murderer. In several respects suicide is more severe than murder. First, suicide contains an open expression of denial of Hashem and of His providence over His creatures; therefore our Sages said that one who deliberately destroys himself has no share in the World to Come. Second, for all sins one can return in teshuva, whereas here he died in the midst of his sin and lost the possibility of regretting his sin. He thinks to himself that by taking his life he will be saved from his suffering, and he does not know that the punishment awaiting him in the World of Truth for deliberately destroying himself is incomparably more severe than all his suffering in this world.

Therefore, even if a person is suffering terrible suffering, he is forbidden to deliberately destroy himself. He must know that everything that happens in the world is done by Divine providence, and everything is for the good. And even if it is very hard for him to bear his suffering, nevertheless he must hope and believe that the wheel will turn for him for the good, and all the suffering will be forgotten as though it had never been. And even if his whole life in this world is hard, nevertheless he must strive to give moral value to his life, and in this merit he will gain eternal life, for all the sufferings of this world are as nothing compared to the eternal reward of the World of Truth.

Despite all that has been said above, we sometimes find that a person is permitted to kill himself, and this is in order not to sin with the most severe sins. These sins are idolatry, forbidden relations and bloodshed. In this spirit a story is brought in the Talmud (Gittin 57b) about Jewish girls who were taken captive to serve as prostitutes all their lives. When they understood that this was what they were destined for, they jumped into the sea and died. And about them the verse was said (Tehillim 68:23): "The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan, I will bring back from the depths of the sea." And they did well, for through their self-sacrifice they were saved from severe sins. And likewise we find with Shaul, king of Israel: in the last battle, in which he was routed before the Philistines, Shaul asked his armour-bearer to kill him so that he would not fall captive to the Philistines, because he knew that they would torture him and humiliate him, and thereby the honour of Israel would be disgraced; and for the sake of the honour of Israel he sought to die by his own hand. Indeed, this act of his is considered a right act of heroism (I Shmuel 31:3-6).

sections.title_en: 10. The Attitude of Halakha to One Who Took His Own Life
sections.body_en:
The attitude of halakha to the act of suicide is very severe, and all the halakhot concerning honour of the dead do not apply to one who took his own life. One does not tear a garment for him as one tears for other dead, one does not eulogise him, and one does not accord him honour. One does not stop work to go to his funeral, and also those who come to the funeral do not come in order to escort him, but in order to honour his relatives, and to stand in a row to comfort them as they leave the cemetery. And likewise one buries the one who took his own life at a distance from the other dead, because such a wicked person is not to be buried beside the other dead (Evel Rabbati 2:1; SA YD 345:1).

There are two main reasons for these halakhot. The first reason is that it is not fitting to accord honour to a wicked person who sinned with the most severe sin of all, self-murder. And there is another reason: to deter people of weak character from thinking about the possibility of escaping the difficulties of their lives through suicide. Sometimes the one who takes his own life wants to hurt his family by his suicide; he wants them to feel guilt over his death and mourn for him. But if he knew from the outset that it would be forbidden to honour him and to do things in his memory, and that according to halakha they could in no way justify his evil act, he would recoil and look for helpful ways to improve his situation. It is known that after a report is published in the media about a person who took his own life, and the background to it is covered without proper criticism of his act, immediately afterwards further reports are published about more people who have put an end to their lives. There is no doubt that the idea of suicide took root in them after they heard about the one who took his own life and were impressed by the media noise that accompanied his death. But if we demonstrate unequivocally our revulsion at acts of suicide, the warped idea of suicide will leave the hearts of those embittered people. Therefore it is forbidden to honour and eulogise the one who took his own life (Glosses of Maharikash YD 345; Nehar Mitzrayim, Laws of Mourning 46).

This is the attitude in principle; but in practice, many times the full halakhic stringency is not applied towards those who took their own lives. The reason for this is that only when it is completely clear that the death indeed occurred deliberately and not by accident is his law that of one who took his own life; but if there is a doubt – perhaps he died in another way, or carried out the act in a moment of insanity – he is not treated as one who took his own life. In addition, many times, for the sake of the family's honour, people try to conceal the fact that their relative took his own life.

Nevertheless, the attitude in principle that appears in halakha towards those who deliberately destroy themselves is known and widely publicised. Even when the public sees that one who took his own life is treated according to the custom for other dead, everyone knows that this is done either because there is some doubt whether perhaps he did not take his own life, or for the sake of the family's honour. But the basic negative attitude towards him remains firmly in place.

sections.title_en: 11. The Law of One Who Took His Own Life
sections.body_en:
The basic principle is that nothing pertaining to the honour of the dead is done for one who took his own life. But what pertains to the honour of the living is done even for one who deliberately destroyed himself. Let us begin to explain in more detail.

The mitzva of burial is fulfilled even for the wicked, including one who took his own life. The reason is that it is forbidden to leave the body of a dead person on the ground without burial. Man was created in the image of God, and as long as his body is disgraced, as it were the honour of Heaven is disgraced with it; and one who leaves the dead without burial transgresses several Torah prohibitions (Sanhedrin 46; SA YD 357).

But one does not bury him together with the other dead, because a wicked person is not to be buried together with upright people (SA YD 362:5). And some wrote that his grave should be distanced more than eight cubits, which are four metres, from the other graves (Gilyon Maharsha YD 345; Gesher Ha-Ḥayim 25:2:4).

There is no need to stop work in order to come and escort the one who took his own life, but one who is free may come to the funeral. After the burial, as they leave the cemetery, those escorting stand in a row and comfort the relatives of the dead, for this is the honour of the living and not the honour of the one who took his own life (SA YD 345:1; Gesher Ha-Ḥayim 25:2:3).

Regarding keri'a (tearing the garment), one must first preface that according to halakha everyone who sees a Jew at the time of his passing is obligated to tear his shirt, as a sign of mourning and grief at the departure of the soul, which is as painful a thing as the burning of a Torah scroll (Shabbat 105b). In addition, all those who mourn the dead are obligated to tear their garment. But regarding a person who deliberately destroyed himself, our Sages said that one does not tear. The great Rishonim disagreed about the question of who does not tear. In the view of the Ramban and the author of the Tur, those who see the act of suicide do not tear, but the family relatives of the one who took his own life tear their garment for him. By contrast, the view of the Rambam is that the family relatives of the one who took his own life are forbidden to tear their garment for him. In the Shulḥan Arukh it was ruled that the halakha follows the Rambam, and even the family relatives of the one who took his own life do not tear for him.

And likewise regarding sitting shiva the poskim disagreed. In the view of the Ramban, the family relatives of the one who took his own life sit shiva for him, because it is their honour to mourn their relative. But in the view of the Rambam and the Shulḥan Arukh, one does not sit shiva for him, because sitting shiva is for the honour of the dead, and one should not honour one who took his own life (SA YD 345:1; Shakh note 2).

In practice, the halakha follows the view of the Rambam, since the Shulḥan Arukh ruled like him. In addition, in every dispute in matters of mourning, the rule is that the halakha follows the lenient view. But one of the great poskim of the Aḥaronim, the author of the Responsa Ḥatam Sofer (YD 326), wrote that where there is grief and disgrace for the family, and they wish to tear and sit shiva for their relative who took his own life, it is permitted to instruct them to tear and sit shiva for him. And this is the practice.

But regarding eulogies, according to all the poskim, since the purpose of a eulogy is to accord honour to the deceased, under no circumstances should one eulogise one who deliberately destroyed himself.

sections.title_en: 12. Saying Kaddish for One Who Took His Own Life
sections.body_en:
A fundamental question in the law of one who deliberately destroyed himself is whether it is fitting to say Kaddish after him. It is known and widely publicised that the purpose of saying Kaddish is for the benefit of the deceased and the repair of his soul, and his merits increase through his sons continuing to sanctify Hashem's Name after his death by saying Kaddish. And since it is widely publicised in the name of our Sages that whoever deliberately destroys himself has no share in the World to Come, if so, seemingly there is no benefit at all in saying Kaddish after him. And so indeed it is commonly said that one does not say Kaddish after one who deliberately destroyed himself. And although it is not said explicitly in the words of our Sages that one who deliberately destroys himself has no share in the World to Come, nevertheless this is accepted in the tradition of Israel. The basis for this is that since murder is one of the three most severe transgressions, and the one who took his own life deprived himself of the possibility of returning in teshuva, his status is consequently that of the greatest wicked person, and therefore he has no share in the World to Come.

In practice, the Ḥatam Sofer wrote (EH 69) that it is fitting to say Kaddish also after one who deliberately destroyed himself. The reason is that even the greatest wicked person has in his foundation some good spark, and it is fitting to repair it and raise it to the World to Come. Something similar we find regarding Avshalom son of David, who was a great wicked man: he rebelled against his father and even wanted to kill him, and lay with his concubines. Nevertheless, after he died, King David prayed for him and said "my son" eight times, in order to raise him from the seven chambers of Gehinnom and bring him up to the Garden of Eden (Sota 10b). And likewise Elisha ben Avuya, who was a sage and departed from the way of the Torah and went down to Gehinnom: it is related of Rabbi Meir that he prayed for him that his punishment in Gehinnom be completed, so that he would merit to rise afterwards to the World to Come (Ḥagiga 15b). Thus we see that prayer and Kaddish can help even great wicked people.

The reason for this is that even regarding the wicked of whom the Sages said that they have no share in the World to Come, the meaning is that every person has the possibility of meriting by right his share in the World to Come through his good deeds, and this they lost, because they sinned with one of the severe sins. But nevertheless they can merit the World to Come through tzedaka and kindness, like those poor who are fed and eat at the table of the rich (Rabbeinu Baḥya, end of Parashat Aḥarei Mot). Therefore it is very fitting that even the son of a wicked person say Kaddish after him, and try to give tzedaka and study Torah for the elevation of his soul; for through his son sanctifying Hashem's Name for the elevation of his soul, the father is judged with kindness and mercy.[2]

notes_en.en:
It should be noted that in the past the custom was that only one person would say Kaddish, and then the right of the orphans of an ordinary Jew who passed away to say Kaddish for their father came before the right of the son of one who deliberately destroyed himself. Therefore many times it did not fall to the son of one who took his own life to say Kaddish for his father. And the Ḥatam Sofer explained that this is why they said that one does not say Kaddish after one who took his own life – that is, his son does not have the power to take a place in the set rota of those who say Kaddish in the synagogue. But if the son of the one who took his own life arranged a minyan for himself in his home, he could say Kaddish after him (Ḥatam Sofer EH 69). But today the custom is that several mourners say Kaddish together, and consequently the son or relative of the one who took his own life also says it with them.
The Ḥatam Sofer further wrote there that one should say Kaddish after him for twelve months. For the reason that for all other dead one says Kaddish for only eleven months is that the judgement of the wicked in Gehinnom is twelve months, and so as not to consider them wicked, one says Kaddish after them for only eleven months. But after one who took his own life, who is certainly called wicked, it is fitting to say Kaddish for twelve months.

sections.title_en: 13. Who Is Considered One Who Deliberately Destroyed Himself?
sections.body_en:
Seemingly, the attitude of halakha towards an act of suicide appears double. But the truth is that there is a difference between the attitude in principle to suicide and the practical application of the halakha. The attitude in principle is that this is the most severe sin, the one who took his own life is a complete wicked person, and nothing should be done for his honour. But in each individual case, the tendency is to try to examine whether it is possible to remove the one who took his own life from the severe and terrible definitions of one who deliberately destroyed himself. Therefore, in practice, most people who appear to have taken their own lives are judged as ordinary dead, for whom all the customs of mourning apply.

First, only when it is one hundred percent clear that that person indeed took his own life is his law that of one who deliberately destroyed himself; but if a doubt still remains, even a slight one, that perhaps he died from an accident or a careless act, then he is judged as an ordinary dead person. Therefore, even if one sees a person where all the signs indicate that he shot himself, since there is no complete certainty that he indeed shot himself intentionally, and there is a certain chance that perhaps a bullet went off by accident, his law is therefore that of an ordinary dead person. Only if he said beforehand that he was about to take his life, or left a letter behind him, is his law that of one who deliberately destroyed himself (SA YD 345:2). And some say that even if he said that he intended to take his life, if he did not do so immediately after his words, his law is not that of one who deliberately destroyed himself, for perhaps he retracted and in the end died without intention (Maharshal; Ḥatam Sofer YD 326).

And some say that the law of one who deliberately destroyed himself applies only if the suicide was carried out by an action after which one dies immediately, such as a person who shoots himself in the head. But if the suicide was carried out by an action after which several moments pass until the moment of death, he is not judged as one who deliberately destroyed himself, for it is possible that after the act he managed to return in teshuva. According to this view, a person who took his life by drowning in a river has the law of an ordinary dead person, because it is possible that after he fell into the river and began to choke, he retracted and had thoughts of teshuva but could no longer save himself. Likewise, one who took his life by cutting his veins – it is possible that in those moments that remained until his death he regretted his rash act, and because of this doubt he is treated as an ordinary dead person (Gilyon Maharsha on SA YD 345; Gesher Ha-Ḥayim 25:3:2). By contrast, some disagree with this and hold that even if he regretted it afterwards, this does not help, since this is not genuine regret, and he retracted only because of his pains and fears (Teshuva Me-Ahava part 3, 409; Zera Emet 3:157).

Sometimes one can judge the one who took his own life favourably, by arguing that perhaps his mind became deranged and he took his life without clear thought; and then he should not be judged as wicked, because he was not responsible for his actions at that time. For example: a person who suffered terrible suffering because of a severe illness – it is possible that his mind became deranged, and as a result he put an end to his life. Another example: it is possible that a person under great stress heard a frightening noise, and since at that time he was in a state of anxiety, he thought to himself that perhaps these were terrorists coming to kill him, and out of great fear he preferred to take his life rather than fall into their hands. Likewise, one can argue that a person who suffered from a tumour in his head was damaged in his brain to the point that he was not responsible for his actions. In all these cases, one can judge the one who took his own life favourably and be lenient in his law, and not treat him according to the law of one who deliberately destroyed himself.[3]

To sum up, whenever it is possible to raise a doubt that perhaps the death occurred by accident, or perhaps the one who took his own life retracted before his death, or that he was not of clear mind, he is treated as an ordinary dead person. And nevertheless, in all these situations, the custom is not to expand in his eulogy.

notes_en.en: In Responsa Besamim Rosh 345 it is written that if a person took his life because of his suffering, his law is not that of one who deliberately destroyed himself, and only one who took his life because he despised his life, in the view of some of the philosophers, is considered one who deliberately destroyed himself. But one must know that many doubt it and hold that Responsa Besamim Rosh is a forgery, and it was not the Rosh who wrote it, but one of the forging maskilim who wrote it and attributed his views to the Rosh. And so the Ḥatam Sofer wrote (YD 326) that this is a view that cannot be, for almost everyone who takes his own life does so because of suffering; and from this halakha the Ḥatam Sofer proved that the book Besamim Rosh is indeed forged. But there were several Aḥaronim who cited it for halakha, because even if we say that the Rosh did not write it, nevertheless, if its words are logical, according to halakha they can be accepted. And indeed several Aḥaronim cited its reasoning for halakha in the law of one who deliberately destroyed himself; and so wrote Sho'el U-meshiv, Mahadura Kamma part 3, 217, and Ḥayim Be-Yad 110 by Rabbi Ḥayim Palagi. In the view of the Maharsham (part 6, 123), whenever it can be argued that he did not know the severity of the prohibition and took his life because of his suffering, he should not be considered one who deliberately destroyed himself; and so wrote Responsa Beit Efrayim YD 76. But the view of most poskim is like the view of the Ḥatam Sofer, that even one who takes his life because of suffering is considered one who deliberately destroyed himself; and so wrote Rabbi Shlomo Kluger in Responsa Tuv Ta'am Va-Da'at 3:202. And in any case, if he was not sane at that time, it appears clearly from the poskim that his law is not that of one who deliberately destroyed himself; and therefore, if his suffering was so harsh that one can attribute it to his mind having become deranged, one may be lenient and not consider him one who took his own life.
